source: Hong & Page (2004) Groups of diverse problem solvers can outperform groups of high-ability problem solvers, PNAS 101(46):16385-16389
finding: Agents are modelled as a perspective plus a heuristic. A group can only get stuck at a point that is a local optimum for every member. Group search is a relay: each agent searches in turn until nobody can improve.
numbers: Group-stuck point = intersection of the members' local optima. Diversity is defined as the share of positions where two heuristics differ, averaged over pairs.
quote: Agents can have diverse perspectives, diverse heuristics, or both.
limits: The framework is general, but the experiment uses identical perspectives and varies only the heuristics. Ability is the average value of the stopping point over all start points, not a task test. Diversity is a hand-made distance between heuristic triples, not a measured trait.
agent_relevance: Frames a thinking schema as a set of search heuristics: the group is stuck only where all heuristics are stuck. This is the formal reason for several different attempts. Under G4 the attempts must differ in the search rule, not only in the sample seed.

source: Hong & Page (2004) Groups of diverse problem solvers can outperform groups of high-ability problem solvers, PNAS 101(46):16385-16389
finding: Computational experiment: agents search a random value function on a circle with a 3-step look-ahead rule. A random group of 10 beats the group of the 10 best agents, and the random group is more diverse.
numbers: Setup: n=2,000 points, values uniform on [0,100], k=3 checks, look-ahead l=12 (1,320 heuristics) or l=20 (6,840 heuristics). Table 1, mean of 50 trials, sd in brackets. 10 agents, l=12: best group 92.56 (0.020), random group 94.53 (0.007); diversity 70.98% vs 90.99%. 20 agents, l=12: 93.78 (0.015) vs 94.72 (0.005); diversity 74.95% vs 91.46%. 10 agents, l=20: 93.52 (0.026) vs 96.08 (0.006); diversity 73.69% vs 94.31%.
quote: We find that a random collection of agents drawn from a large set of limited-ability agents typically outperforms a collection of the very best agents.
limits: The landscape is a random value function, so there is no structure for an expert to exploit. The gap shrinks when the group grows to 20 because the best-20 group becomes more diverse. Random groups win by about 1 to 2.6 points on a 100-point scale near a ceiling of about 95.
agent_relevance: Shows the effect is real in this toy: a pooled set of weak but unlike searchers beats strong but alike searchers. The size of the gain is small in absolute terms.

source: Hong & Page (2004) Groups of diverse problem solvers can outperform groups of high-ability problem solvers, PNAS 101(46):16385-16389
finding: Single-run detail shows how little individual ability separates the groups and how much diversity does. The best group is more able but alike.
numbers: l=12 representative run: best agent 87.3, worst agent 84.3; mean of the 10 best 87.1, mean of 10 random 85.6; collective value 93.2 (best 10) vs 94.7 (random 10); mean pairwise diversity 0.72 vs 0.92. With l=20 there are 6,840 agents (20x19x18).
limits: One run, not the 50-trial mean. The pool is finite, so the top group is forced to share heuristics (reordered triples of the same numbers).
agent_relevance: The top-ranked attempts from one model are near copies. Choosing the best-scoring samples to vote on gives a group like the best 10: high ability, low diversity. This is the G4 situation.

source: Hong & Page (2004) Groups of diverse problem solvers can outperform groups of high-ability problem solvers, PNAS 101(46):16385-16389
finding: Theorem 1: with probability one there exist sample sizes N1 < N such that N1 random agents beat the N1 best of N drawn agents. It rests on four assumptions: (i) agents never move to a worse point, (ii) no agent solves the problem alone, (iii) for every non-optimal point some agent can improve it, (iv) the best agent is unique.
numbers: Result is a limit statement: no values of N or N1 are given.
limits: With a very large pool the best N1 agents are all copies of the single best agent, so they add nothing. The theorem says nothing about how fast the effect appears.
agent_relevance: The logic is simple: top-ranked agents in a large pool are clones of one agent. Under a single model the same logic applies to top-ranked samples. The lesson is to avoid clone attempts, not that weak attempts beat strong ones.

source: Thompson (2014) Does Diversity Trump Ability? An Example of the Misuse of Mathematics, Notices of the AMS 61(9)
finding: Thompson (a mathematician) says Theorem 1 has little mathematical content and does not apply to the experiment. She shows the original Lemma 1 is wrong and needs V to be one-to-one. She calls the diversity-trumps-ability reading a leap.
numbers: Die example: six agents, group A of 50 drawn from the 6 vs the best 50 of 10,000 draws from the same 6. So N1=50 and N=10,000. In the limit the best 50 are copies of one agent. The experiment (n=2,000, l=20, k=3, 6,840 agents) does not meet the theorem's assumptions.
quote: the paper contains a theorem that has neither mathematical content nor real-world applications
limits: A critique by one author; Page and Megginson answered in letters (2015). Romaniega (2025) says the replies did not address the technical point.
agent_relevance: Warns the agent designer: the proof is trivial, so do not cite it as evidence that mixing weak solvers helps in general.

source: Thompson (2014) Does Diversity Trump Ability? An Example of the Misuse of Mathematics, Notices of the AMS 61(9)
finding: Thompson reproduced the simulation (n=2,000, l=20, k=3). She confirmed that 10 random agents beat the 10 best. She then showed that maximum-diversity groups do worse than random groups, so diversity as defined is not the cause.
numbers: Her run: diversity score summed over 45 pairs was 131 for 10 random agents and 120 for the 10 best. Groups built to have maximal diversity scored below the median of 200 random groups of 10.
quote: a maximally diverse group performed less well than the median performance of 200 random groups of ten agents
limits: Code only on request; no exact group scores printed. She used her own random function since Hong-Page did not report theirs. Her point is about attribution, not about the sign of the effect.
agent_relevance: Supports a careful reading: the benefit comes from random draws spreading over many different heuristics, not from a diversity score. A schema should sample varied approaches, not maximise a distance number.

source: Thompson (2014) Does Diversity Trump Ability? An Example of the Misuse of Mathematics, Notices of the AMS 61(9)
finding: Thompson's hostility argument: the diversity rating is just how many of three entries differ between heuristics. Rename it hostility and the same data say hostility trumps ability. The label proves nothing.
numbers: Same simulation, same numbers: the random group had 131 vs 120 on the disagreement score; relabelled hostility, it is the more hostile group.
limits: Rhetorical point; shows the construct validity problem of a hand-made diversity metric.
agent_relevance: When our agent reports diversity of attempts, it must use a defined measure linked to error coverage (do different attempts fail on different items), not a word count or style distance.

source: Romaniega (2025, v3) Fatal errors and misuse of mathematics in the Hong-Page theorem and Landemore's epistemic argument, arXiv:2307.04709
finding: Full re-examination of the theorem. Clones of the same agent add nothing by assumption, so the compared groups are all useful distinct agents versus the best agent, with no true random selection. Gives counterexamples when technical assumptions (V injective, unique best agent) are dropped. Proves a mirror theorem: ability trumps diversity.
numbers: Sections: counterexamples for V injective (2.1), unique best agent (2.2), clones (2.3-2.4); new theorem in section 3. Says Page's reply to Thompson did not address the injectivity point, and Landemore kept using the theorem after 2014.
limits: One author; econ.TH preprint v3, January 2025. Not shown as peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: Adds a clean statement: if ability is high enough that top agents cover all needed moves, ability wins. Diversity helps only when the top agents are clones.

source: Romaniega (2025) on replies to Thompson: Kuehn (2017) and Singer (2019)
finding: Romaniega lists two replies to Thompson that he considers unanswered on the technical point: Kuehn 2017 (Critical Review 29(1), a note on Thompson's challenge) and Singer 2019 (Diversity, not randomness, trumps ability, Philosophy of Science 86(1):178-191). Grim et al. 2019 builds on Hong-Page.
numbers: Only the existence and citation details were read.
limits: Singer's and Kuehn's own texts were not opened (paywalled; web search budget ended). Secondhand: do not quote their numbers from this line.
agent_relevance: Marks the debate: Singer argues diversity, not randomness, explains the effect; Thompson argues the opposite. Treat the question as open for the schema.

source: Grim, Singer, Bramson, Holman, McGeehan & Berger (2019) Diversity, ability, and expertise in epistemic communities, Philosophy of Science 86(1):98-123
finding: Extends Hong-Page to landscapes with different degrees of randomness. The diversity-trumps-ability result is sensitive to how random the landscape is. The authors advise against reading the result too broadly.
numbers: Only the abstract (Cambridge Core page) was read. The replication README by Wallrich says the strategy comparison needed 56,700 runs, each testing up to 24,360 heuristics from 2,000 start points.
quote: demonstrate the sensitivity of the diversity trumps ability result
limits: Landscape correlation values and group scores NOT read; the full paper was blocked (403, archive rate limit). Do not quote specific numbers from this paper until a full text is opened.
agent_relevance: Confirms a boundary condition that matters for us: on structured problems, where expertise pays, ability wins. Most benchmark tasks have structure.

source: Wallrich replication of Hong & Page (2004) and Grim et al. (2019), GitHub README
finding: An open mesa agent-based replication of both models exists. The README says the Hong-Page simulation runs on a laptop in hours; the Grim et al. sweep needs cloud compute.
numbers: 56,700 runs for the strategy comparison; up to 24,360 heuristics per run; 2,000 start points; 22.5 hours on a 32-core VM.
limits: README only; the analysis notebook and its results were not opened. Whether it reproduces the published numbers is not stated.
agent_relevance: Code exists if we want to test our own landscape toy before building a schema operator.

source: Hong & Page (2004) with Thompson (2014): combined boundary conditions
finding: Boundary conditions that both texts expose: (1) random value function with no structure; (2) deterministic local-search agents that stop at local optima; (3) a very large pool so the top group is clone-heavy; (4) a perfect relay with no communication cost; (5) the answer is a number you can check, so the group keeps the best found.
numbers: Read from the HP text (assumptions i-iv, relay search, uniform [0,100] values) and Thompson's critique.
limits: Synthesis of two primary texts; not a new experiment.
agent_relevance: The benefit needs (a) real variety in search rules, (b) a way to detect which attempt is better, (c) a hard problem where one rule gets stuck. If the task is easy or has one right route, extra attempts add little.

source: Li, Lin, Xia & Jin (2025) Rethinking Mixture-of-Agents: is mixing different LLMs beneficial? (Self-MoA), arXiv:2502.00674
finding: Mixing different LLMs (Mixed-MoA) is often worse than aggregating several samples of the single best model (Self-MoA). Quality matters more than cross-model diversity.
numbers: AlpacaEval 2.0 length-controlled win rate: Self-MoA on WizardLM-2-8x22B beats Mixed-MoA by 6.6 points; 2-layer Self-MoA 65.7 vs 2-layer Mixed-MoA 59.1. Average gain 3.8% across MMLU, CRUX, MATH. Single models: WizardLM 53.1, Qwen1.5-110B 43.9, Qwen1.5-72B 36.6, LLaMA-3-70B 34.4, Mixtral-8x22B 30.2, dbrx 25.4.
limits: Gain depends on one model clearly being best. On a mixed task (MMLU+CRUX+MATH, Table 6) mixing can help: proposers 'mmmddd' average 60.04 vs 54.74 for the best single-model Self-MoA (d). The aggregator is still an LLM; no verifier.
agent_relevance: This is the LLM version of ability-beats-diversity. With one model (our case), several samples of the best model beat a mix with weaker ones when the task is one type.

source: Li et al. (2025) Self-MoA: quality-diversity regression
finding: Over 200 experiments they regress Mixture-of-Agents accuracy on proposer quality and on proposer diversity (Vendi score). Both matter; the quality coefficient is larger on every dataset.
numbers: Table 4 (normalised coefficients): MMLU quality 2.558 (se 0.176), diversity 1.841, R2 0.771; CRUX quality 4.548 (0.459), diversity 1.421, R2 0.685; MATH quality 4.719 (0.416), diversity 2.839, R2 0.760. All p < 0.001.
limits: Linear fit only; diversity measured by Vendi score on output text; six proposers per prompt. Mixtures are not independent runs.
agent_relevance: A rare direct estimate of the ability-versus-diversity trade-off for LLMs: a unit of quality is worth about 1.4 to 3.2 units of diversity here. Do not trade accuracy for variety.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Mixture-of-Agents enhances large language model capabilities, arXiv:2406.04692
finding: Layered MoA with six open models reaches 65.1% LC win rate on AlpacaEval 2.0 vs 57.5% for GPT-4 Omni. Different-model proposers beat sampling the same model.
numbers: Table 3 (2 layers, Qwen1.5-110B aggregator): n=6 multiple-proposer 61.3% vs single-proposer 56.7%; n=3 58.0% vs 56.1%; n=2 58.8% vs 54.5%; n=1 47.8%. MoA-Lite 59.3%.
limits: Single-proposer uses temperature sampling of the same model; Li et al. later got the opposite result using the strongest model as the repeated proposer. Judged by a GPT-4 annotator, which may prefer blended or longer answers.
agent_relevance: The pro-diversity side that Self-MoA challenges. The two papers disagree because the proposer pools differ in quality.

source: Naik et al. (2024) Diversity of thought improves reasoning abilities of LLMs (DIV-SE), arXiv:2310.07088
finding: A single model is asked to list distinct approaches and personas, and each approach becomes a different prompt. Voting over these varied prompts beats ordinary self-consistency at lower cost on planning and graph tasks.
numbers: Table 1, GPT-4 zero-shot CoT: Graph Coloring CoT 15.0, SC-10 23.0, IDIV-SE 74.0, DIV-SE 97.0. Blocksworld 3: CoT 70, SC-10 73, IDIV-SE 82, DIV-SE 94. Blocksworld 4/5: CoT 40, SC-10 41.2, IDIV-SE 57, DIV-SE 69.6. AQuA-RAT gains of 9.84 and 14.6 points over baselines of 71.9% (few-shot CoT) and 70.47% (zero-shot CoT), section 4.1.1; which variant produced them was not checked.
limits: Diversity comes from prompts, not models; the approaches are written by the same LLM, so errors still correlate. Biggest gains are on tasks where plain sampling is nearly one-way (graph colouring, planning).
agent_relevance: Strongest evidence that diversifying the search rule (prompted approach) beats only resampling. This is Hong-Page's heuristic diversity inside one model. It stays within G4 if used for exploration plus a check, not as independent votes.

source: Hegazy (2024) Diversity of thought elicits stronger reasoning capabilities in multi-agent debate frameworks, J Robot Auto Res 5(3)
finding: Multi-agent debate (after Du et al.) is better with different model families than with copies of one model. After 4 rounds, a diverse set of medium models passes GPT-4 on GSM8K.
numbers: GSM8K singles: Gemini-Pro 78%, PaLM 2-M 64%, Mixtral 7x8B 70%. Diverse debate, 4 rounds: 91%. Three copies of Gemini-Pro: 78% to 80% (no CoT) or 82% (zero-shot CoT). ASDiv singles: Gemini Flash 1.5 89%, Gemini Pro 86%, GPT-3.5 81%; diverse debate reaches 94%.
limits: Small single-author paper, no confidence intervals. Debate also changes the compute used, so the comparison partly measures number of calls. The models have similar ability, which is Hong-Page's condition.
agent_relevance: Counter to Self-MoA, but with near-equal models. Under a single-model rule (G4) this advantage is not available; self-debate does not give it.

source: Maryanskyy, Budnikov & Kaliyev (2026) When agents disagree: the selection bottleneck in multi-agent LLM pipelines, arXiv:2603.20324
finding: Resolves the Mixture-of-Agents vs Self-MoA split by aggregation quality: diversity helps only if the selector can pick the best candidate. A closed-form crossover threshold is derived.
numbers: 42 tasks in 7 categories, N=210. Diverse team plus judge-based selection: win rate 0.810 against a single-model baseline (Opus-only). Homogeneous team: 0.512, Glass's delta 2.07. Majority vote 0.496. MoA-style synthesis 0.179; selection beats synthesis by +0.631; synthesis preferred in 0 of 42 tasks. Adding a weaker model improved results and cut cost (p<1e-4, not pre-registered).
limits: Judges are LLMs and the authors admit partial circularity; an independent-judge rerun keeps the direction (Spearman 0.90) but lowers win rates. One lab, one baseline model.
agent_relevance: The closest recent test of Hong-Page for LLM teams: diversity works if the aggregator selects. Fits our schema: generate varied attempts, then verify or select by evidence, never blend them.

source: Hu, Lau, Liu, Chen, Ng & Low (2025) Dipper: diversity in prompts for producing LLM ensembles in reasoning tasks, arXiv:2412.15238
finding: Feed one small model several optimised system prompts in parallel, chosen to be both good and different. Three Qwen2-Math-1.5B instances with different prompts beat a 7B model of the same family on MATH.
numbers: Seven-prompt ensemble 57.31% on MATH vs best single prompt 55.76% and mean single prompt 56.55% (Qwen2-Math-1.5B). Spearman correlation between their diversity-fidelity score and ensemble accuracy up to about 0.8. n=9 gives about +10 points (about 20% relative) over the single model.
limits: Gain over the best single prompt is only about 1.5 points; larger only against the unprompted single model. Small models; numbers read from the running text, table cells not re-checked.
agent_relevance: A way to choose which varied prompts to include: score each by quality and by how unlike it is, as Hong-Page's ability plus diversity.

source: Kim, Garg, Peng & Garg (2025) Correlated errors in large language models, arXiv:2506.07962
finding: Different LLMs share many wrong answers. Diversity across providers is less than assumed. More accurate models have more correlated errors.
numbers: Data: 349 LLMs on 12,032 leaderboard questions, and 20 LLMs on 1,800 resume-job pairs. On the HELM data, two models that are both wrong pick the same wrong choice about 60% of the time (random choice would give about 33%).
limits: Multiple-choice setting, so agreement is easier than in free text. Regression drivers (shared architecture, provider) were only skimmed.
agent_relevance: If different models already agree on errors 60% of the time, samples of one model agree more. This is the quantitative basis for G4 and for the limit of what a second model adds.

source: Jiang et al. (2025) Artificial Hivemind: the open-ended homogeneity of language models, arXiv:2510.22954 (NeurIPS 2025 D&B)
finding: On 26K open-ended real queries (Infinity-Chat), models repeat themselves and also write alike across model families. Average pairwise embedding similarity of answers to the same prompt typically exceeds 0.8 at top-p 0.9 and temperature 1.0.
numbers: Dataset: 26K queries, 6 categories, 17 subcategories, 31,250 human annotations, 25 annotators per example. Similarity above 0.8 also at the paper's second, more random setting (temperature 2.0, lower top-p).
limits: Open-ended tasks without a ground truth; embedding similarity is a proxy for diversity. Not a test of problem-solving accuracy.
agent_relevance: Turning up temperature does not buy independent attempts. For exploration, vary the prompt or the strategy, not the temperature.

source: Park, Schoenegger & Zhu (2023) Diminished diversity-of-thought in a standard large language model, arXiv:2302.07267
finding: GPT-3.5 (text-davinci-003) replicated Many Labs 2 studies with almost no variation across runs (the correct answer effect), so it cannot stand in for a population of different people.
numbers: 14 Many Labs 2 studies; 8 could be analysed; 37.5% of the original results and 37.5% of the Many Labs 2 results replicated. In the Moral Foundations survey it called itself conservative in 99.6% of runs, and liberal in 99.3% in the reverse-order condition.
limits: One old model; the six unanalysable studies had zero or near-zero variance. Newer models not tested here.
agent_relevance: A single model is one voter, not a crowd. Repeated runs give a spread of wording, not a spread of views.

source: O'Brien, Fazelpour, Rubin & Wong (2025) Epistemic monocultures and the effect of AI personalization, CogSci 2025
finding: Agent-based model on an NK epistemic landscape where agents can ask an AI. A shared, non-personalised AI cuts the community's diversity and hurts results. Personalisation gives mixed results.
numbers: Follows the Lazer & Friedman (2007) NK model; social learning rate held at 25%; outcome includes loss of transient diversity. Cited survey figure: 1,600 researchers, 66% expect AI to help process data, 69% fear overreliance on pattern recognition.
limits: The text extract was two-column and partly garbled; abstract and set-up were read, the result tables were not. Simulation only.
agent_relevance: A model of the shared-AI problem: when everyone queries the same model, the group converges early. One agent can do the same to itself if each step reuses the same prior.

source: Weisberg & Muldoon (2009) Epistemic landscapes and the division of cognitive labor, Philosophy of Science 76(2):225-252
finding: Agent-based model of scientists on an epistemic landscape (hills of significance). Compares followers (copy successful neighbours), mavericks (avoid visited places) and controls. From memory of the literature, mixing in some mavericks helps; this was not verified here.
numbers: Not read; no numbers. The PDF was blocked and the web search budget was used up.
limits: Key unopened source. Alexander, Himmelreich & Thompson (2015) criticise landscape results as dependent on setup; also not read.
agent_relevance: Needed for a maverick operator. Check the paper before use; do not rely on this line.

source: Lazer & Friedman (2007) The network structure of exploration and exploitation, Administrative Science Quarterly 52(4):667-694
finding: NK-landscape model where agents learn from neighbours. As described by O'Brien et al. (2025): more social learning gives faster early gains but leaves less time exploring, a speed versus long-run best trade-off.
numbers: Not read; no numbers.
limits: Secondhand through one citing paper.
agent_relevance: Supports a slow-mixing schema: keep attempts apart for a while before sharing results.

source: Reijula & Kuorikoski (2019) The diversity-ability trade-off in scientific problem solving, Philosophy of Science
finding: Listed in a search result as arguing that the Hong-Page model is inadequate for studying the diversity-ability trade-off. Not opened.
numbers: No numbers; one-line summary from a search listing only.
limits: Not read; the web search budget ended and the PDF sat behind a proxy.
agent_relevance: Read before citing. Treat as a critique of the model, not as data.

source: Page (2007) The Difference: How the power of diversity creates better groups, firms, schools, and societies; Princeton University Press
finding: Book-length statement of the diversity-trumps-ability claim and its policy uses. Thompson cites p.165 as where Page states it as a general claim.
numbers: Not read. Thompson quotes page 165.
limits: Per Thompson and Romaniega, the book goes beyond the 2004 paper's assumptions.
agent_relevance: Source of the broad claim the schema should not copy.
